name: Pricing Illiquid Assets
title: Pricing Illiquid Assets
answer: Pricing illiquid assets covers positions that do not trade on an active exchange, such as private AI company equity, venture fund interests, restricted stock, intellectual property, data rights, and thinly traded tokens. The core problem is that no continuous market price exists, so a portfolio must rely on periodic valuations that can lag true economic value. This work sits inside portfolio construction because the assigned price affects position sizing, risk limits, performance reporting, and capital allocation across the AI economy.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on internal valuation systems that combine cap table data, transaction records, document repositories, and scenario models. Teams typically use secure data rooms for source documents, spreadsheets or dedicated valuation software for cash flow and comparables, and portfolio accounting systems that store fair value hierarchies. Where tokenized assets are involved, blockchain oracles and on-chain trade data may feed the same valuation pipeline, but the core infrastructure remains the controlled environment where assumptions are logged and versioned.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners mark illiquid positions to model rather than to market, using discounted cash flow, comparable company or transaction multiples, option pricing for contingent claims, and waterfall analysis for structured interests. Machine learning can assist by imputing missing comparables, clustering similar private companies from filing text, or estimating volatility from sparse secondary trades, but the final valuation is usually reviewed by a human. Monte Carlo simulation and scenario weighting are common when exit timing or milestone payments are uncertain.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on the fair value hierarchy, where Level 1 inputs are quoted prices, Level 2 are observable inputs, and Level 3 are unobservable assumptions that require the most disclosure. Valuation policies set who can approve a mark, how often it is refreshed, and what evidence must be retained, because conflicts of interest arise when a portfolio manager also supplies the price. Provenance matters for every input, from a broker quote to a cap table entry, and model risk management requires documenting why a method was chosen and how sensitive the result is to key assumptions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more frequent marks, tokenization of private interests that creates thin but real secondary liquidity, and automated valuation models that blend alternative data with traditional comparables. Portfolio systems are likely to integrate illiquid pricing directly into risk and exposure reporting rather than treating it as a separate quarterly exercise. At the same time, regulators and auditors are pressing for more transparent Level 3 disclosures, so the future will pair faster valuation with stronger audit trails and provenance controls.
